cells.tense: The crossing is underway and you are here, present, standing at the water's edge.
cells.ask: Name one thing worth carrying into what comes next, and one you're done carrying. Say both to one person this week, plainly, and let the leaving stand without defense.
cells.core:
You know what to attend to here, and it doesn't come as argument. Something lands and something doesn't, and the landing is quieter than you'd expect. You've walked far enough that leaving a piece of what you gathered costs you, and you're still walking. That's the picture: a threshold made of your own meaning, and you're not pretending it's easy.
This place, where you know what matters before you can explain why, is doing exact work in this room — turning you toward the connection that runs deeper and away from the one that only looks familiar. You can rely on it. What you turn toward is early and it is yours.
cells.sheetLine: You know what's worth carrying, and you're already walking.
cells.verb: walking toward the deeper connection on the far side of what you've gathered
cells.place: where you know what deserves your attention before you can say why

cells.tense: You are already on the far side, arriving somewhere that hasn't been built yet.
cells.ask: End one conversation tonight without getting them across. Let what you meant sit unfinished, and do nothing with the quiet that follows.
cells.core:
You're ahead of the crossing. Out in front there's a version where the people around you already understand what you're walking toward, and you're camped there — so a talk becomes a case for leaving, a room becomes a place to move them before you've moved. The bracing gives it away. You're readying for a threshold that hasn't arrived, and the readying is spending what you'd need to walk it.
This place, where you know what matters before you can explain why, pushed this hard, attends to all of it at once — defending, explaining, outrunning a reaction that may not come. Pace flattens what matters into what's urgent. Slow down enough to let the crossing be the crossing, and the far side stops needing your defense.
cells.sheetLine: You're bracing for a threshold you haven't reached.

cells.tense: You are at a door that is already behind you, still in the old room.
cells.ask: Pick one pattern you keep watching — a person, a job, a room — and write what it's doing on one page. Then choose what in it belongs to you.
cells.core:
You can see what matters, and you've stopped letting it steer. It still shows up — quick, accurate, gone before you use it — but the walking and the seeing have come apart, and the old room keeps a hold on you that way, not through ignorance. Something there passes for understanding and doesn't move anybody, including you.
When this place runs thin, the sense of what deserves attention goes quiet and everything weighs the same. At full strength it looks like this: you walk into a room and know within a minute what the room is actually about, and you act on it without needing a reason. You don't force yourself to care more. You look at one pattern hard enough that it becomes visible as a pattern, and let that visibility pull.
cells.sheetLine: You still know what matters. You've stopped letting it steer.

cells.tense: You are steering this crossing already, and you describe it as something happening to you.
cells.ask: Find one choice you've been filing under circumstances — what to stop, where to turn, who to keep — and say aloud that you chose it. To yourself first.
cells.core:
Look at where you've been turning for a while now. That isn't drift. You've been attending to things on purpose — the friend you keep giving time to, the question you keep returning to, the thing you quietly stopped feeding. This place is in it. But you tell it as if the current carried you, as if the leaving were done to you rather than by you.
The steering is real and it's yours. What's missing is only the claim. Take one of those turns and say it was you, and you're back at the pen — not writing a different life, admitting you've been writing this one.
cells.sheetLine: This is yours already. You haven't claimed it yet.

attempts.check: The record doesn't say the person has actually left anything — Passage may be a threshold they're approaching, not a departure already made, so Too Little must not assert a room where saying it went badly. A reader could reasonably say they haven't crossed anything yet, they're just tired, and the cell should let that stand without collapsing. The ask survives being wrong because each one is a small act that teaches pattern-attention regardless of whether the read is true. The sentence that serves the writer more than the person is any line about 'what you're really carrying,' and I've kept that out.
